analysis.one_liner: Requires carmakers to share vehicle repair data, information, and tools with owners and independent repair shops.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan right-to-repair bill with 56 cosponsors cleared a House subcommittee by voice vote in November 2023, but the full Energy and Commerce Committee never took it up and it died when the Congress ended without any floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The REPAIR Act would force car and truck manufacturers to let vehicle owners — and the independent shops and parts makers they choose — access the data their vehicles generate about diagnostics, repair, and maintenance, without fees or special manufacturer devices. It would bar manufacturers from blocking compatible aftermarket parts or steering owners to brand-name parts, tools, and dealer service, and it would put the Federal Trade Commission in charge of enforcing those rights, with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration setting security standards for data access. The bill died in committee and never became law.
analysis.who_benefits: Vehicle owners and lessees, who could get their cars fixed at any shop, use any qualified parts, and choose their own towing service without manufacturer lock-in. Independent repair shops, independent parts stores, aftermarket parts and tool manufacturers, and remanufacturers would gain access to the repair data and tools that manufacturers currently control, letting them compete for repair work that now flows to dealerships. Drivers in rural areas far from a dealer service center would gain nearby repair options.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Car owners and independent repair shops

how_it_helps.text: Manufacturers could not use technological barriers (like software locks or encryption requiring a manufacturer device) or legal barriers (like contract clauses or waivers) to stop owners, their chosen repair shops, or aftermarket parts makers from accessing vehicle-generated repair data or critical repair information and tools [S3].

Vehicle-generated data would have to be provided to owners and their designees 'without restrictions or limitations (including a fee, license, or requiring use of a device mandated by the motor vehicle manufacturer),' and if a car transmits data wirelessly, the owner could get it directly from the vehicle through a standardized access platform [S3].

Outside of recalls and warranty repairs, manufacturers could not mandate or imply a mandate to use a particular brand of parts, tools, or equipment, and any recommendation would have to carry a plain-language notice that owners can choose their own parts [S3].

Owners could use the towing or service provider of their choice, and independent facilities could diagnose, repair, and maintain vehicles 'in the same manner as any motor vehicle manufacturer or motor vehicle dealer' [S3].

The FTC would enforce the law: anyone could file a complaint, the FTC would have to investigate and issue a final order within five months, and contract clauses that try to waive these rights would be void [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Motor vehicle manufacturers would bear the cost: they would have to open repair data and tools at fair, reasonable, and nondiscriminatory cost, build and secure a wireless standardized access platform, run owner notifications, and comply with FTC and NHTSA rulemaking. They would also lose the leverage that steers out-of-warranty repair revenue to their own parts, tools, and dealer service centers. Consumers could see some of the compliance cost passed into vehicle prices.

drawbacks.text: Opening real-time, wireless access to vehicle data creates a cybersecurity risk the bill itself acknowledges: it carves out the right of manufacturers to keep 'cryptographic or technological protections necessary to secure vehicle-generated data, safety critical vehicle systems, and vehicles,' and it directs NHTSA to write security standards before the access platform goes live [S3]. Opponents of open telematics access have argued it could be exploited for vehicle theft or tracking.

Implementation would be steered largely by industry: the FTC's advisory committee reserves eleven appointed seats for industry sectors — manufacturers, dealer service centers, parts makers, insurers, trucking — against a single seat for consumer rights organizations, and the independent entity administering data access would be built from a 'cross-section of industry stakeholders' [S3].

Enforcement is complaint-driven and soft: a manufacturer that fixes the specific conduct complained of 'shall be relieved of liability' for that violation, and no private right of action is created — owners depend on FTC action within a five-month order deadline [S3].

Relief would be slow. Data access rules take effect on enactment, but the wireless standardized access platform and its administrator would not be in place until roughly two years after NHTSA and FTC finish their rulemakings [S3].

The bill would preempt state laws in places — including any state law mandating particular brands of parts or tools — raising the concern that a federal floor could displace stronger state right-to-repair rules [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core bargain is strong for drivers: cheaper, more competitive repair options against real but manageable costs for automakers, which already control the security architecture and could retain encryption protections. The honest weaknesses are in the design, not the goal — industry-heavy implementation bodies, complaint-only enforcement with no private lawsuit option, and a multi-year wait for the wireless data platform all soften what the bill delivers. On balance it is a consumer bill with genuine guardrails, weakened at the edges.

outcome.mechanism: The bill died in committee: a House subcommittee approved it by voice vote in November 2023, but the full Energy and Commerce Committee never marked it up and it never reached the House floor before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Neal Dunn (R-FL) introduced the REPAIR Act on February 9, 2023, with three original cosponsors from both parties — Rep. Brendan Boyle (D-PA), Rep. Warren Davidson (R-OH), and Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-WA) — and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1] [S3] [S5].
It was referred the same week to the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce, where it sat for more than eight months [S5].
On November 2, 2023, the subcommittee held a mark-up session and forwarded the bill to the full committee by voice vote — a step with no recorded opposition [S5].

That was the bill's last action. The full Energy and Commerce Committee never held a markup or vote, the bill never received a House floor vote of any kind, and no Senate action ever occurred; the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with the bill dead [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers came out ahead: by letting the bill expire in committee, they kept control of vehicle-generated repair data, critical repair information, and tools, and preserved the flow of repair work and parts sales toward manufacturer channels and dealer service centers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Automakers, whose repair data control survives

sides.party_line_note: Support was evenly bipartisan from the start — 28 Democrats and 28 Republicans among 56 cosponsors, with a bipartisan group of four original sponsors — and the subcommittee advanced it by voice vote; no one ever had to cast a recorded vote against it.

industries.note: The bill would strip manufacturers of their gatekeeper control over vehicle-generated data, repair software, and tools, and would bar them from steering owners to their own parts and service. Out-of-warranty repair and parts are a major profit stream for automakers and their dealer networks, which is why an industry-wide lobby fought to keep such mandates off the books.

Shops would get the same diagnostic data, repair procedures, software, and tools as dealers, letting them fix late-model, software-heavy cars they increasingly cannot service. That means more competition and closer, often cheaper repair options for drivers.

industries.industry: Aftermarket parts and tool manufacturers and remanufacturers
industries.note: The bill would prohibit manufacturers from blocking compatible aftermarket parts and from brand mandates in repair manuals, protecting the aftermarket's ability to sell parts that work with modern vehicles.
Dealer service centers would lose a captive share of out-of-warranty repair work as owners gain real choices, though dealers would face new duties to inform buyers of their rights at purchase.
